audits.question: Check the entry's evidence for Sumerian/Akkadian language contact and the separation of scribal language survival from spoken-language replacement; which dated text or scholarly passage supports the institutional coupling?
audits.entry_locator: corpus/knowledge/civilizations/mesopotamia-sumer-akkad.md line 36 (table row 'Contact ecology' in '## Language family and typological contrast'), line 38 (grammatical-anchors note incl. 'the timing of vernacular loss are incompletely recoverable'), line 48 (Sumerian word-signs inside Akkadian writing do not identify the spoken language); craft grid row 'Ritual language survives vernacular change' at line 166.
audits.entry_claim: Bounded entry assertion (line 36): "Sumerian and Akkadian coexisted and influenced one another; Sumerian remained a learned and cultic language after ordinary spoken use declined", with guardrails "a script's survival does not prove a speech community's survival" (line 36) and "Exact pronunciation, Sumerian dialect geography, and the timing of vernacular loss are incompletely recoverable" (line 38). The entry claims no precise death date and names no single dated primary text as witness for the coupling; its named scholarly anchors are Jagersma (2010) and Huehnergard (2011).
audits.source_citation: Wikipedia contributors, "Sumerian language", Wikipedia (online encyclopedia article text as retrieved 2026-10-17; tertiary mediation — the article's underlying scholarly references were not independently inspected this round).
audits.source_locator: Lead section, third paragraph ("Akkadian, a Semitic language, gradually replaced Sumerian...") with its closing sentence on mutual grammatical and vocabulary influence; infobox 'Era' field ("Went out of vernacular use around 1700 BC; used as a classical language until about 100 AD"); 'Proto-literate period' paragraph on unresolved language attribution.
audits.source_excerpt: Akkadian, a Semitic language, gradually replaced Sumerian as the primary spoken language in the area c. 2000 BC (the exact date is debated), but Sumerian continued to be used as a sacred, ceremonial, literary, and scientific language
audits.retrieval_method: FetchURL of the public article page (English text, no authentication); host web-search quota was exhausted, so targets were reached by direct URL entry.
audits.basis: Every leg of the bounded row is covered by retrieved article text: (i) coexistence and mutual influence — the same lead paragraph's "whose grammar and vocabulary were significantly influenced by Sumerian, and vice versa"; (ii) learned/cultic survival after spoken decline — the quoted excerpt plus the infobox "used as a classical language until about 100 AD"; (iii) the entry's script-versus-speech guardrail — the article situates continuing Sumerian textual use inside "Akkadian-speaking Mesopotamian states", i.e. a written register persisting beyond the spoken community, and marks the timing "(the exact date is debated)"; (iv) early-attribution caution — "there remains some scholarly disagreement about whether the language written with it is Sumerian at all". Nothing retrieved contradicts the row.
audits.coupling_implication: Supports the entry's stage-separation rule (line 69: spoken language, scribal register, royal ideology, temple organization on separate layers) and design-grid row "Ritual language survives vernacular change" (line 166): a fictional culture can lawfully sustain a learned, cultic register inside an alien vernacular without equating script persistence with a surviving speech community and without fixing a precise death date for the older tongue.
audits.limits: Tertiary mediation: the retrieved text is an encyclopedia article, not a collated dated text, and its cited scholarship was not independently inspected; no primary cuneiform witness was retrieved this round (the entry itself names no single dated text for the coupling, and the fetched ETCSL catalogue page returned a bare composition list with no usable prose). Jagersma's Leiden repository record was retrieved but supplies the author's abstract only — logged as metadata corroboration, not passage proof, mirroring the entry's own abstract-only caution for Zawadzki (line 22). Britannica, Smarthistory and Michalowski's Michigan page returned HTTP 403; MET pages returned HTTP 429; the OIS 4 PDF path returned 404; failed access stays unresolved and identity metadata never became content confirmation. The verdict stays inside the entry's own calibration: vernacular-loss timing remains modeled, not newly dated.

extra_corroboration.source_citation: Jagersma, Abraham Hendrik (2010). A Descriptive Grammar of Sumerian. PhD dissertation, Leiden University — repository record and author's abstract.
extra_corroboration.retrieved_text_status: Author's abstract retrieved 2026-10-17: "Although Sumerian became obsolete as a living language about four thousand years ago, it continued to be used as a language of scholarship and cult until the end of the first millennium BC." Abstract text is cover/metadata level, not body-text confirmation; the full-text PDF path was not obtainable from the extracted page.
extra_corroboration.note: This is the entry's own named anchor (lines 15 and 38); the abstract matches the entry row on survival-after-decline, and the record's stated descriptive corpus ("about 2500 to 2000 BC") matches the entry's line-15 corpus note.

extra_corroboration.source_citation: Wikipedia, "Sumerian language", proto-literate-attribution sentence (same URL as the main source; listed separately only to document this adjacent entry caution).
extra_corroboration.retrieved_text_status: Retrieved 2026-10-17: "there remains some scholarly disagreement about whether the language written with it is Sumerian at all".
extra_corroboration.note: Corroborates the adjacent entry assertion at line 44 ("assigning every earliest record securely to Sumerian overstates decipherment"); not an independent witness — same retrieved page as the main source.

audits.question: Check its kaunakes or tufted/skirt-dress terminology against a dated object or scholarly source; distinguish modern/Greek descriptive naming, pictured texture and actual fibre/garment construction.
audits.entry_locator: corpus/knowledge/civilizations/mesopotamia-sumer-akkad.md line 139 (costume table row 'Early Dynastic votive and elite imagery' with its limit column), adjacent rows 'Gudea statues' (line 141) and 'Institutional textile records' (line 142), craft rule at line 149, museum locators at lines 27 and 187.
audits.entry_claim: Bounded entry assertion (line 139): Early Dynastic votive and elite imagery shows "Wrapped or skirt-like garments, conspicuously textured/flounced surfaces", under the limit "Carved texture does not uniquely establish fleece, woven pile, tufting, or construction; state any reconstruction as a proposal and check it object by object rather than settling on one reading." Recorded limit per the round selection rule: the word 'kaunakes' does not occur in this entry — its terminology is 'textured/flounced surfaces'; the Greek-derived term appears only in the read-only sibling file corpus/knowledge/culture-material/dress-through-eras.md line 30 ("tufted kaunakes skirts (a Greek word describing the fleece look)") and in round-1 triage corpus/lessons/round-1-triage/Z16.md line 14. This audit cross-references those read-only and does not edit them.
audits.source_citation: Fashion History Timeline (Fashion Institute of Technology), entry "Kaunakes", quoting Daniel Delis Hill, The History of World Costume and Fashion (2011), p. 19; Kemper, Costume (1977), p. 34; François Boucher, 20,000 Years of Fashion (1987), p. 34; and Phyllis Tortora, "Ancient World: History of Dress" (pp. 51–59 as cited by the Timeline). The quoted books were not inspected; the Timeline page is the retrieved mediator (English).
audits.source_locator: Timeline paragraphs quoting Tortora (votive figures' skirts 'appear to be' sheepskin; tufted simulations; Greek word applied to both types), Kemper (tufts of wool threaded through a coarsely woven cloth panel — a construction proposal), and Boucher ('referred not to a material but to a form').
audits.source_excerpt: Sumerian devotional or votive figures often depict men or women wearing skirts that appear to be made from sheepskin with the fleece still attached... The Greek word kaunakes has been applied to both sheepskin and woven garments of this type.
audits.retrieval_method: FetchURL of the public Timeline page (no authentication); the URL's reachability was additionally confirmed by the corpus's own round-1 triage record corpus/lessons/round-1-triage/Z16.md line 14.
audits.basis: (i) Dated-object leg: retrieved tertiary text keys the textured skirt to named dated objects (Wikipedia kaunakes: Statue of Iku-Shamagan, King of Mari, c. 2500 BCE; votive relief of Ur-Nanshe, Early Dynastic III 2550–2500 BC; Khafajah female statuette 2650–2550 BCE), and the Timeline's Tortora quote keys the type to 'Sumerian devotional or votive figures'. (ii) Pictured-texture-versus-construction leg: Tortora's skirts that 'appear to be made from sheepskin with the fleece still attached' stand beside garments that 'simulate sheepskin' with attached tufts — two live readings of one pictured texture, exactly the entry's non-uniqueness guardrail; Kemper's tufted-wool-through-woven-panel recipe is phrased as one proposal, not a confirmation. (iii) Naming leg: 'The Greek word kaunakes has been applied to both sheepskin and woven garments of this type' (Tortora via FIT) and 'the term kaunakes was still applied to this garment, and thus referred not to a material but to a form' (Boucher via FIT) separate the modern/Greek label from any fibre claim. No retrieved text asserts a unique construction, so the entry's object-by-object caution is supported rather than contradicted.
audits.coupling_implication: Confirms the entry's craft rule (line 149: specify garment shape, fiber, finish, fastening, maintenance, access, and occasion independently): a fictional Early-Dynastic-like textured skirt may be modelled as fleece-wrapped, tuft-simulating, or woven-pile, and the pictured texture licenses none of these uniquely; a fictional culture's native garment term should not be back-projected from the Greek-derived scholarly label, which names a form rather than a material. Designers keep the reconstruction visible as a proposal per object.
audits.limits: The construction question remains open by design: retrieved sources offer competing proposals and confirm none for any specific object, consistent with the corpus's round-1 triage (corpus/lessons/round-1-triage/Z16.md line 14, 'no single authoritative construction reading'). The named specialist study — Breniquet, "Que savons-nous exactement du kaunakès mésopotamien?", Revue d'assyriologie et d'archéologie orientale 110 (2016): 1–22 — was identified bibliographically but not retrievable this round; its title counts as bibliography only, not passage support. First-hand museum dress description was not obtained: MET 59.2 returned HTTP 429 on repeated attempts (left unresolved), Smarthistory and Britannica returned 403, a guessed Louvre ark URL resolved to the wrong object (an Elamite brick, discarded), and the retrieved Cleveland 1963.154 record (c. 2144–2124 BCE) describes clasped hands and temple placement but omits garment texture, so it serves as object locator only. The Timeline's figure captions did not survive text extraction, so its internal object accessions are not individually cited. Wikipedia's kaunakes article carries a March-2024 self-flagged 'appears to contradict itself' banner and is used as tertiary corroboration only. Cleveland's own page dates the statue c. 2144–2124 BCE while the entry (line 187) records differing Met 59.2 / Cleveland 1963.154 estimates; the Met estimate remained unfetchable, so that spread stands as recorded, not updated.

extra_corroboration.source_citation: Wikipedia, "Kaunakes" (tertiary; citing Breniquet 2016, Tortora & Eubank 2010, CAD vol. 5 p. 134), retrieved 2026-10-17.
extra_corroboration.retrieved_text_status: Retrieved text includes: "It was only around 2,500 BC that the sheepskin garment was replaced by a textile made of woven wool; however, the tuft part of the dress was continued by 'sewing tufts onto the garment or by weaving loops into the fabric'. The Greeks called this dress kaunakes."
extra_corroboration.note: Independently reproduces the naming-versus-material separation and the dated-object chronology; used as corroboration only because the article carries a self-flagged contradiction banner (March 2024).

extra_corroboration.source_citation: Cleveland Museum of Art, "Statue of Gudea", accession 1963.154 (museum-object record, dated c. 2144–2124 BCE), retrieved 2026-10-17.
extra_corroboration.retrieved_text_status: Object record retrieved; its description covers the clasped-hands gesture, the ensi (governor) title of Lagash, temple placement as stand-ins, and the mistaken 20th-century head completions (1963.680) — it does not describe the garment's texture or construction.
extra_corroboration.note: Confirms the entry's object locator (line 27) and its line-141 caution ('Compare individual objects; damaged or restored heads are unreliable costume evidence'), but supplies no dress-terminology passage; recorded as access limit, not support.
